source: GetYourGuide checkout programme. Every line comes from the checkout case study (/work/checkout.html): experiment log, key decisions, narrative and validation notes.
programme: All experiments were A/B tests with statistical significance thresholds, 120K to 140K users per variant across the programme, guardrail metrics tracked throughout. Figures are directional reconstructions of relative effects; exact values are confidential.

calls.title: Hold-your-spot countdown: "We'll hold your spot for 30:00"
calls.context: Travellers reached the total, doubted the price and looped back to check it. 38% of eventual converters left checkout at least once mid loop.
calls.hypothesis: Showing the real hold time would turn urgency into reassurance at the moment of paying.
calls.risk: Any countdown can read as pressure if it stops being honest.
more: The timer showed the existing hold time. Artificial scarcity ("only 2 left") was the option the team rejected.
Still visible on the live checkout, captured on mobile in August 2026.
calls.why: Urgency reframed as service: the spot is reserved for the traveller, not used against them. It was the top single win of the programme.
calls.lesson: Urgency builds trust only when it is true and on the user's side.

alt.iterate: Testing copy or duration before a full rollout is reasonable caution with any urgency mechanic.
alt.kill: Being wary of countdowns in checkout is a sound instinct. What changed the call here is that the timer reflected a real hold.

calls.title: Price-expiry countdown: "Book now, the price rises when the timer ends"
calls.context: The hold-your-spot timer (EXP-01) was already live. This tested the opposite framing of the same mechanic.
calls.hypothesis: A price deadline would push hesitant travellers to pay sooner.
calls.risk: The trust guardrail fell and refund intent rose.
more: Trust was one of the guardrail metrics tracked throughout the programme.
Same mechanic as EXP-01, opposite framing: one timer serves the user, this one threatens them.
calls.why: The click was won, but trust and refund intent moved the wrong way. A win that spends trust is a loss with a delay. Killed on principle and on data.
calls.lesson: Not every conversion gain creates business value.

alt.ship: A +4.2% lift is real, and many teams ship on the primary metric. The guardrail is what turned this one.
alt.iterate: Looking for a framing that keeps the click without the threat is reasonable. The team already had that version live as EXP-01.

calls.title: Promo code as a quiet link instead of an open field
calls.context: An open promo code field sat in the middle of checkout, just before paying.
calls.hypothesis: A quiet link would stop mid checkout coupon hunting without hiding the option.
calls.risk: Travellers who do have a code need one more tap.
calls.why: An empty field is an invitation to leave and go coupon hunting. A link keeps the option without issuing the invitation.
calls.lesson: Remove the invitation to leave, not the option.

alt.iterate: Checking that travellers with a code still find the link is a fair follow up.
alt.kill: Protecting people who have a discount is a fair concern. The code stayed one tap away, which is why the team saw no cost.

calls.title: Single-page checkout: collapse every step into one view
calls.context: On mobile each step was a separate page load, and every transition cost 8 to 12% of remaining users.
calls.hypothesis: If reloads broke the flow, removing the steps altogether would remove the leak.
calls.gain: A cleaner flow, neutral on desktop.
calls.risk: Slower and worse on mobile, the segment that carried the programme.
more: 65% of traffic was mobile, and 72% of the programme's uplift came from mobile.
Responsive tweaks to the old three step flow were also rejected: the drop off at each transition was too large for tweaks.
What shipped instead: two named steps, with progress, timer and order summary kept across the boundary (EXP-02).
calls.why: You do not trade your best segment for elegance. The idea was killed, but its principle survived: unbroken context, shipped as two named steps.
calls.lesson: Read the segment that carries the result, not the average.

alt.ship: A simpler flow that held on desktop is tempting, and simplicity has long term value. Mobile is where the cost landed.
alt.iterate: This is close to what happened. The single page died, but the principle behind it came back as two named steps.

calls.title: Email-first continue, account creation deferred
calls.context: New travellers met a create account step before they could pay.
calls.hypothesis: Asking only for an email to continue would lift new user conversion.
calls.risk: Dropping an idea while its problem is still visible in the sessions.
calls.why: The number was flat, but the qualitative signal survived. v2 paired email first with SSO and moved account creation after purchase: +1.1%, shipped.
calls.lesson: Flat is not dead when the qualitative signal survives.

alt.ship: Shipping a neutral change that simplifies the flow is defensible when it costs nothing.
alt.kill: Killing a flat test is the textbook move. The recordings are what kept this one alive.

calls.title: Reorder payment methods to match each market
calls.context: Credit card showed first in every market. In the Netherlands 72% of online payments use iDEAL; in Poland, BLIK dominates.
calls.hypothesis: Leading with each market's preferred method would lift payment completion.
calls.gain: A clean win where it worked.
calls.risk: A global rollout forces an answer only half the markets supported.
more: Methods adapted per market, iDEAL in the Netherlands, BLIK in Poland, Sofort in Germany, with the preferred one expanded by default.
Built as geo IP ordering: one system, not four manually maintained market pages.
calls.why: Not a global truth, a local one. It became a per market rollout with a shared default, instead of forcing one answer on four markets.
calls.lesson: A local truth deserves a local rollout.

alt.ship: Shipping everywhere is defensible when the flat markets lose nothing. The team kept a shared default instead of one global answer.
alt.kill: Two flat markets out of four is a fair reason for doubt. The clean wins in the other two are what kept it.
